s.dp: Communication › Mock, Ridicule
s.d: to make fun of someone by joking or jesting{N:001}
s.g: to scoff; to jeer; to joke at

s.dp: Communication › Mock, Ridicule
s.d: to make fun of someone by joking or jesting{N:001}
s.g: to scoff; to jeer; to joke at

s.dp: Time › Units of Time with Reference to Other Units or Points of Time: Yesterday, Today, Next Day
s.d: a day prior to the time of a discourse

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: (an idiom, literally: yesterday, today, and forever) an unlimited extension of time, from the past into the future
s.g: always; eternally; past and present and future

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Lend, Loan, Interest, Borrow, Bank
s.d: to give something to someone for use, with the expectation that the same or its equivalent will be returned

s.dp: Think › To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
s.d: to choose or select, presumably by a group and possibly by the actual raising of the hand
s.g: to choose; to elect; to select

s.dp: Control, Rule › Assign to a Role or Function
s.d: to formally appoint or assign someone to a particular task
s.c: In ⟦Acts 14:23|Acts 14:23⟧ χειροτονέω may, however, be understood in the meaning of ‘to choose or elect to office by the raising of hands’ (see LN 30.101).

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Bad, Evil, Harmful, Damaging
s.d: (comparative of {L:κακός<SDBG:κακός:000000>}[a] ‘bad,’ {D:88.106}) pertaining to being worse in the sense of being harmful and damaging

s.dp: Value › Good, Bad
s.d: pertaining to being less satisfactory than something else

s.dp: Artifacts › Images and Idols
s.d: in the NT the image of the winged creature that stood over the covenant box (but in certain OT contexts, supernatural winged creatures)
s.c: Since it is difficult to employ a satisfactory descriptive equivalent of χερούβ, most translators have simply employed a borrowed term and have described the appearance of the χερούβ in a glossary or marginal note. In English, however, it is impossible to use ‘cherub,’ since cherubs are known simply as ‘baby angels’ (typical of Valentine cards). In some English translations the plural form of χερούβ, namely, ‘cherubim,’ has been employed, but for some persons cherubim is a singular with an analogically formed plural cherubims. In general, for χερούβ one can best employ a phrase, either ‘the image of a winged creature’ or ‘a winged creature.’

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Kinship Relations Based upon Marriage
s.d: a woman whose husband has died
s.c: In rendering ⟦Mark 12:42|Mark 12:42⟧ ‘poor widow’ may be translated as ‘poor woman whose husband had died.’

s.dp: Military Activities › Soldiers, Officers
s.d: a military officer, normally in command of a thousand soldiers

s.dp: Number › Pair, Group [Numbered Collectives]
s.c: Normally, however, ἐν δέκα χιλιάσιν is simply translated as ‘with ten thousand soldiers.’|In ⟦Revelation 5:11|Revelation 5:11⟧ the implication is that each group consists of a thousand each, but the expression ‘thousands upon thousands’ is really a way of emphasizing the enormous number. In a number of languages the equivalent would be ‘millions’ or ‘an exceedingly large number.’

s.dp: Number › One, Two, Three, Etc. [Cardinals]
s.d: cardinal number, where there are one thousand instances of a countable entity

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: an island, with a city of the same name, in the Aegean Sea

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: a basic inner garment worn under the {L:ἱμάτιον<SDBG:ἱμάτιον:000001>}[b] ‘cloak’ ({D:6.172})

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: any kind of clothing

s.dp: Natural Substances › Water
s.c: In the NT χιών occurs only as a symbol of complete whiteness, and hence in those cases in which a receptor language may not have any term for snow, it is possible to use a nonfigurative expression such as ‘very, very white.’ In a number of languages, however, there may not be a specific term for snow but a type of descriptive phrase reflecting people’s knowledge about snow, even though the substance may not occur in their immediate vicinity. For example, in some instances snow is spoken of as ‘volcano frost.’ In certain parts of the world, however, the translator’s problem is not in finding a term for snow but in distinguishing between a number of different terms which designate distinct types of snow and snow formations. Under such circumstances one can simply use for ‘snow’ an expression which suggests the whitest variety or that form of snow which is most commonly referred to.

s.dp: Artifacts › Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
s.d: a loose outer garment worn by Roman soldiers and travellers
s.c: In some parts of the world the closest equivalent of χλαμύς is a poncho.

s.dp: Features of Objects › Hot, Lukewarm, Cold
s.d: pertaining to being somewhere between hot and cold

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person whose family members reported to Paul about divisions in the church in Corinth

s.dp: Features of Objects › Color
s.d: light green, green (typical of plants){N:001}

s.dp: Features of Objects › Color
s.d: pale greenish gray (evidently regarded as typical of a corpse, since the color is used as a symbol of death){N:001}

s.dp: Plants › Plants That Are Not Trees
s.d: (semantic derivative of χλωρός[a] ‘green,’ {D:79.34})
s.c: In a number of languages it would seem redundant to speak of ‘green plants,’ since all plants are regarded as being green. It may therefore be more satisfactory to employ a rendering such as ‘nor any plant,’ referring in this instance to larger annual plants or bushes, in contrast with both grass and trees.

s.dp: Natural Substances › Earth, Mud, Sand, Rock
s.d: (derivative of {L:χοῦς<SDBG:χοῦς:000000>} ‘dust,’ {D:2.15}) pertaining to being made or consisting of dust or soil
s.g: made of dust; made of soil
s.c: Though in general χοῦς and the derivative χοϊκός would seem to refer to dry dust, they may also refer to dirt or soil. In ⟦1 Corinthians 15:47|1 Corinthians 15:47⟧ it is more appropriate to speak of the creation of Adam as ‘made from the ground’ or ‘formed out of soil.’ For another interpretation of χοϊκός in ⟦1 Corinthians 15:47|1 Corinthians 15:47⟧, see LN 1.42.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › The Earth's Surface
s.d: pertaining to having the nature of earthly existence in contrast with that which is heavenly or of heaven
s.g: of earth; earthly; made of earth
s.c: It may even be possible in rendering χοϊκός in ⟦1 Corinthians 15:47|1 Corinthians 15:47⟧ to say ‘created out of earth’ or ‘made from dust’ (see LN 2.16).

s.dp: Spacial Dimensions › Specific Measures of Volume
s.d: a dry measure of approximately one quart or one liter
s.c: The Greek text of ⟦Revelation 6:6|Revelation 6:6⟧ has literally ‘denarius’ (see LN 6.75), but it is preferable in translating ⟦Revelation 6:6|Revelation 6:6⟧ to relate a denarius to its buying power in terms of a day’s wages for an average worker.

s.dp: Animals
s.d: hairy four-legged mammal with hoofs, brown or gray in color; non-ruminant and omnivorous; Sus scrofa; domesticated land animal; unclean, not to be eaten; regarded as an ugly, filthy, and destructive animal and often associated with pagan rituals
s.c: Though references to pigs in the OT frequently involve very strong connotations of uncleanness and disgust, references in the NT are somewhat more neutral. However, in the story of the Prodigal Son (⟦Luke 15:15|Luke 15:15⟧) the reference to the task of feeding swine certainly indicates the desperate condition of the younger brother. Some translators have found it necessary to indicate such a fact by a marginal note, since the language into which the translation is being made may reflect a very different cultural attitude from that which occurs in the Scriptures. For example, in certain areas of New Guinea, one who is responsible for taking care of pigs is an individual with relatively high social status.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Anger, Be Indignant With
s.d: to have a strong feeling of displeasure and antagonism as the result of some real or supposed wrong
s.g: to be very angry; to be full of anger
s.c: In a number of languages expressions for ‘anger’ are highly idiomatic, for example, ‘his abdomen burned against,’ ‘to be bitter toward,’ or ‘to become red against.’

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Physiological Products of the Body
s.d: the bitter yellowish liquid secreted by the liver and stored in the gall bladder
s.c: It is possible, however, that in ⟦Matthew 27:34|Matthew 27:34⟧ the reference is not specifically to gall but to a substance with an especially unpleasant taste.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Envy, Jealousy
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to be in the gall of bitterness) to be particularly envious or resentful of someone
s.g: to be very jealous; to be terribly envious; to be bitterly envious

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a city in Galilee

s.dp: Help, Care For › Provide For, Support
s.d: to make available whatever is necessary to help or supply the needs of someone
s.g: to provide for; to support; to supply the needs of; provision; support

s.dp: Linear Movement › Dance
s.d: patterned rhythmic movements of the whole and/or parts of the body, normally to the accompaniment of music
s.c: In a number of languages there are highly specific terms for various types of dancing, and one must make certain that the appropriate expression is used. Some terms for dancing may refer only to erotic dances; others, to highly ritualized performances in drama or religious practice; and still others may refer to personal expressions of happiness, joy, or grief. Special care must be exercised in selecting a term which will fit the context.

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: to cause to eat so as to become satisfied
s.g: to cause to eat one’s fill; to satisfy with food
s.c: In some languages one may translate χορτάζω in ⟦Matthew 15:33|Matthew 15:33⟧ as ‘to cause to have as much as they wanted’ or ‘to give them food so that they didn’t want any more.’|In ⟦Matthew 5:6|Matthew 5:6⟧ (ὅτι αὐτοὶ χορτασθήσονται ‘because they will be satisfied’) the occurrence of χορτάζω should be interpreted as figurative, for it does not have specific reference to being satisfied with food (see LN 25.82).

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: to eat, resulting in a state of being satisfied
s.c: One may render ‘were satisfied’ as ‘had all you wanted to eat’ or ‘did not want to eat any more.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Content, Satisfied
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of χορτάζομαι[a] ‘to eat one’s fill,’ {D:23.15}) to be satisfied or content with some object or state
s.g: to be satisfied; to be content with

s.dp: Foods and Condiments › Food
s.d: any kind of food or nourishment{N:001}
s.c: Almost all languages have at least a few general terms for food, though these may be derived from verbal expressions meaning essentially ‘that which is eaten.’ In some instances a distinction may be made between ‘that which is chewed’ and ‘that which is drunk,’ and it may therefore be important in certain contexts to speak of food in general by a phrase meaning ‘that which is either chewed or drunk.’ If one fails to include both types of food, the reader might interpret a passage such as ⟦Matthew 6:11|Matthew 6:11⟧ as requesting only solid foods.|In the place of a general term or phrase such as ‘that which is eaten’ or ‘that which is consumed,’ some languages generalize the meaning of a particular term. For example, in certain parts of the Orient the term meaning specifically ‘rice’ also refers to ‘food’ in general. In fact, some persons will declare, ‘I have not eaten!’ if they have not had rice as part of a meal. A similar type of meaning has developed in English with respect to ‘bread.’ For example, in rendering ⟦Luke 4:4|Luke 4:4⟧ (οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος ‘man shall not live by bread alone’) it would be wrong to employ a strictly literal rendering, since this might mean simply that people should not live on a diet consisting solely of bread. The meaning of ⟦Luke 4:4|Luke 4:4⟧ is, of course, ‘to live means more than merely eating.’

s.dp: Plants › Plants That Are Not Trees
s.d: small green plants (and in NT contexts referring primarily to green grass in a field or meadow)
s.c: In referring to small green plants, a number of languages employ two quite different terms, one indicating specifically grass (with leaves having parallel veins) and the other designating all other types of annual plants (those having branching veins in the leaves). In ⟦Matthew 13:26|Matthew 13:26⟧ it is important to employ a term which would include grass and other plants with parallel veins, since the weeds in this passage imitate the appearance of wheat, which does have parallel veins in the leaves.

s.dp: Plants › Non-Fruit Parts of Plants
s.d: the young growth of a plant arising from a germinating seed{N:001}
s.c: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between different kinds of ‘sprouts.’ Certain sprouts have only a single blade (for example, grass), while others are double (as in the case of beans). In ⟦Mark 4:28|Mark 4:28⟧ the reference is to a grass-like plant with a single blade

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the husband of Joanna, a follower of Jesus

s.dp: Natural Substances › Earth, Mud, Sand, Rock
s.d: dust, soil (see also {D:2.16})
s.c: ‘Shake the dust from your feet’ may be expressed as ‘kick the dust from your feet.’ In some instances, however, the more appropriate equivalent would be ‘get rid of the dust from your feet’ or even ‘remove the dust from your feet and leave it there.’

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Behavior, Conduct
s.d: to conduct oneself in a particular manner with regard to some person

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Behavior, Conduct
s.d: to behave or to conduct oneself with respect to certain means
s.g: to deal with; to have dealings with

s.dp: Perform, Do › Do, Perform
s.d: to engage in the activity of making use of something
s.g: to use; to make use of

s.dp: Case › Instrument
s.d: to make use of instruments{N:001}
s.c: In ⟦Acts 27:17|Acts 27:17⟧ βοηθεία is best regarded as a technical nautical term for supports (ropes or cables) used in aiding a ship in danger (see LN 35.10).

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Need, Lack
s.d: (derivative of {L:χρῄζω<SDBG:χρῄζω:000000>} ‘to lack,’ {D:57.39}) that which is lacking and particularly needed

s.dp: Mode › Should, Ought
s.d: that which should be or happen, with the implication of need or lack to be made up

s.dp: Perform, Do › Do, Perform
s.d: an activity which is needed

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Owe, Debt, Cancel
s.d: a person who is in debt

s.dp: Mode › Should, Ought
s.d: that which should be or happen, with the implication of propriety

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Need, Lack
s.d: to lack something which is necessary and particularly needed
s.g: to need; to lack; to be without

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Be Rich, Be Wealthy
s.d: economic resources, usually implying an abundance of such assets

s.dp: Artifacts › Money and Monetary Units
s.d: a generic term for currency, occurring mostly in the plural
s.g: money (normally a reference to actual coins); coin; change
s.c: It would also be possible to translate ἤνεγκεν τὸ χρῆμα in ⟦Acts 4:37|Acts 4:37⟧ as ‘he brought the proceeds from the sale.’|In ⟦Acts 8:18|Acts 8:18⟧ (προσήνεγκεν αὐτοῖς χρήματα ‘he offered them money’) the reference of χρήματα would appear to be cash.

s.dp: Know › Well Known, Clearly Shown, Revealed
s.d: to make known a divine revelation
s.g: to make known God’s message; to reveal a message from God

s.dp: Communication › Name
s.d: to give a name or title to
s.g: to call; to give a name to; to give a title to

s.dp: Know › Well Known, Clearly Shown, Revealed
s.d: (derivative of {L:χρηματίζω<SDBG:χρηματίζω:000000>}[a] ‘to make known a divine revelation,’ {D:28.39}) the content of a divine revelation or utterance{N:001}

s.dp: Value › Useful, Useless
s.d: pertaining to having a valid use or function
s.c: In some languages, χρήσιμος in ⟦2 Timothy 2:14|2 Timothy 2:14⟧ may be expressed as ‘helpful.’ For example, ‘it is of no use’ may then be rendered as ‘it isn’t helpful’ or ‘it does not help.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sexual Relations
s.d: the sexual function or use of the same or opposite sex
s.c: It is often possible to refer to ‘natural sexual function’ as ‘sexual relations with the opposite sex’ or ‘men having sexual relations with women.’ ‘That which is contrary to nature’ may be expressed often as ‘men having sexual relations with men’ and ‘women having sexual relations with women.’ In many societies homosexuality is almost unknown, but there are always ways of speaking about such relations in a euphemistic manner.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Kindness, Harshness
s.d: to provide something beneficial for someone as an act of kindness
s.g: to act kindly; to be kind; kindness

s.dp: Communication › Language Levels
s.d: eloquent and attractive speech involving pleasing rhetorical devices

s.dp: Value › Good, Bad
s.d: pertaining to being superior for a particular purpose or use
s.c: In a number of languages it may be necessary to translate ⟦Luke 5:39|Luke 5:39⟧ as ‘the old wine tastes better’ or ‘the old wine is fine to the taste’ or, in an idiomatic expression, ‘the old wine makes the tongue dance.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Goodness
s.d: pertaining to being useful and benevolent

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Kindness, Harshness
s.d: (derivative of {L:χρηστεύομαι<SDBG:χρηστεύομαι:000000>} ‘to act kindly,’ {D:88.67}) pertaining to being kind
s.c: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘God is kind’ is ‘God is good to’ or ‘God does what is good for.’

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Easy, Light
s.d: pertaining to that which is pleasant or easy, with the implication of suitability
s.c: In a number of languages it is necessary to translate χρηστός by a negativized equivalent, for example, ‘it is not difficult to bear.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Goodness
s.d: an event or activity which is useful or benevolent
s.g: that which is useful; what is benevolent; benevolence
s.c: In the case of χρηστός (LN 88.9) and χρηστότης, an equivalent often contains an expression meaning ‘to help.’ For example, the expression ‘what is useful’ is often rendered as ‘that which helps people’ or ‘that which proves good for people.’

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Kindness, Harshness
s.d: to provide something beneficial for someone as an act of kindness
s.g: to act kindly; to be kind; kindness

s.dp: Control, Rule › Assign to a Role or Function
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of χρῖσμα ‘to anoint,’ not occurring in the NT) to assign a person to a task, with the implication of supernatural sanctions, blessing, and endowment
s.g: to anoint; to assign; to appoint; assignment; appointment
s.c: It is rare that one can employ a literal rendering of χρίω or χρῖσμα in such contexts as ⟦Luke 4:18|Luke 4:18⟧ and ⟦1 John 2:20|1 John 2:20⟧, since ‘to pour oil upon someone’ as a means of conveying a supernatural blessing and endowment for a task is culturally very rare. A strictly literal rendering of χρίω or χρῖσμα as ‘to pour oil upon’ is likely to be interpreted either as an insult or as an event preparatory to setting a person on fire and thus to destroy or to torture. Accordingly, in place of a literal rendering of χρίω or χρῖσμα, it is often necessary to employ some such expression as ‘to be appointed by God’ or ‘to be given a special task by God.’

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Religious
s.d: one who is identified as a believer in and follower of Christ

s.dp: Religious Activities › Roles and Functions
s.d: (literally: one who has been anointed) in the NT, titles for Jesus as the Messiah, but in many contexts, and especially without an article, Χριστός becomes a part of the name of Jesus; see {D:93.387})
s.c: In a number of languages Χριστός (or Μεσσίας) as a reference to the Messiah occurs in a transliterated form based either on Χριστός in Greek or on Messiah in Hebrew. However, in some languages an attempt is made to represent the significance of the terms Χριστός and Μεσσίας by translating ‘God’s appointed one’ or ‘God’s specially chosen one’ or ‘the expected one,’ in the sense of one to whom everyone was looking for help and deliverance.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: (the Greek translation of the Hebrew and Aramaic word ‘Messiah’) a proper name for Jesus; see also {D:53.82}

s.dp: Control, Rule › Assign to a Role or Function
s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of χρίω ‘to anoint,’ not occurring in the NT) to assign a person to a task, with the implication of supernatural sanctions, blessing, and endowment
s.g: to anoint; to assign; to appoint; assignment; appointment
s.c: It is rare that one can employ a literal rendering of χρίω or χρῖσμα in such contexts as ⟦Luke 4:18|Luke 4:18⟧ and ⟦1 John 2:20|1 John 2:20⟧, since ‘to pour oil upon someone’ as a means of conveying a supernatural blessing and endowment for a task is culturally very rare. A strictly literal rendering of χρίω or χρῖσμα as ‘to pour oil upon’ is likely to be interpreted either as an insult or as an event preparatory to setting a person on fire and thus to destroy or to torture. Accordingly, in place of a literal rendering of χρίω or χρῖσμα, it is often necessary to employ some such expression as ‘to be appointed by God’ or ‘to be given a special task by God.’

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
s.d: to extend a state or an event beyond an expected time

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: to spend a considerable period of time in a state or activity
s.g: to spend a long time in; to stay a long time

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: an indefinite unit of time (the actual extent of time being determined by the context){N:001}

s.dp: Time › A Point of Time without Reference to Other Points of Time: Time, Occasion, Ever, Often
s.d: points of time consisting of occasions for particular events
s.c: In a number of languages there is no general term for ‘time’ or ‘occasion.’ In some contexts it is simply not necessary to have such a term. For example, in rendering ⟦Matthew 13:30|Matthew 13:30⟧ one may translate ‘when the harvest comes, I will say to the reapers’ or ‘when people begin to harvest, I will say to the reapers.’ In other contexts, a term which normally refers to some unit is employed in a generic sense, as in the case of Greek ὥρα which means literally ‘hour’ but is frequently used as a generic expression for a point of time, as in ⟦Matthew 8:13|Matthew 8:13⟧. In ⟦Acts 7:17|Acts 7:17⟧ χρόνος may often be rendered by a generic expression such as ‘day,’ for example, ‘when it was almost the day for God to keep his promise.’ In the case of ⟦Matthew 26:45|Matthew 26:45⟧, the nearness of the time may be indicated as ‘very soon the Son of Man will be handed over.’|Though it seems quite ordinary in English for one to speak of ‘time coming’ or ‘… drawing near,’ this type of figurative usage is impossible in many languages. The equivalent may be simply ‘will soon be’ or ‘is about to happen.’ The expression οὔπω ἥκει ἡ ὥρα μου (literally ‘my time has not yet come’) in ⟦John 2:4|John 2:4⟧ denotes that it is not yet the occasion for a particular event (see καιρός in ⟦John 7:8|John 7:8⟧ and compare ⟦John 7:10|John 7:10⟧) but that it will soon be. In these contexts the expression may be rendered as ‘there is still time’ or ‘I will soon do it.’ In ⟦John 7:30|John 7:30⟧ and ⟦John 8:20|John 8:20⟧ (οὔπω ἐληλύθει ἡ ὥρα αὐτοῦ ‘his time has not yet come’) the reference is to the occasion of his eventual arrest, implying that it will indeed happen.

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
s.d: an exceedingly long period of time from an assumed beginning up to the present
s.g: since all time; from all ages past; from the beginning of time

s.dp: Time › Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
s.d: to experience a duration of time
s.c: In a number of languages χρονοτριβέω may be best rendered as ‘to remain for a time’ or idiomatically as ‘to sit for a time.’

s.dp: Natural Substances › Metals
s.d: gold (the most highly valued metal in the ancient world)
s.c: Terms for gold are widespread throughout the world even as the presence of gold or knowledge about gold is likewise almost universal. Therefore, there is usually no difficulty involved in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘gold.’

s.dp: Artifacts › Adornments
s.d: object or objects made of gold{N:001}
s.c: Gold jewelry may be referred to as ‘pretty things made out of gold,’ but rather than say that the woman was ‘covered with gold ornaments’ (⟦Revelation 17:4|Revelation 17:4⟧), it may be far more appropriate to say ‘she wore many gold ornaments’ or ‘many gold ornaments were fastened to her clothes.’

s.dp: Artifacts › Money and Monetary Units
s.d: (an idiom, literally: silver and gold) a generic expression for currency

s.dp: Artifacts › Adornments
s.d: pertaining to the wearing of a gold ring

s.dp: Natural Substances › Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
s.d: chrysolite (yellow quartz or yellow topaz), golden yellow in color (see {D:2.29})

s.dp: Natural Substances › Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
s.d: chrysoprase, a greenish type of quartz (see {D:2.29})

s.dp: Natural Substances › Metals
s.d: gold (the most highly valued metal in the ancient world)
s.c: Terms for gold are widespread throughout the world even as the presence of gold or knowledge about gold is likewise almost universal. Therefore, there is usually no difficulty involved in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘gold.’

s.dp: Artifacts › Money and Monetary Units
s.d: gold money, gold coin{N:001}

s.dp: Natural Substances › Metals
s.d: (derivative of {L:χρυσός<SDBG:χρυσός:000000>}[a] ‘gold,’ {D:2.49}) pertaining to being made or consisting of gold

s.dp: Activities Involving Clothing and Adorning
s.d: to be adorned with gold objects
s.g: to be adorned with gold; to be dressed with gold; to be covered with gold adornments
s.c: In ⟦Revelation 17:4|Revelation 17:4⟧ the phrase κεχρυσωμένη χρυσίῳ involves semantic redundany or what one may also speak of as semantic reinforcement.

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: skin or surface of the human body
s.c: In a number of languages a clear distinction must be made between the skin of an animal and the skin of a human being. A further distinction is often made between skin as a part of a living animal or human and skin which has been removed from the body and presumably made into leather (see δέρμα, LN 6.184).

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Sickness, Disease, Weakness
s.d: pertaining to a disability that involves the imperfect function of the lower limbs

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Land in Contrast With the Sea
s.d: dry land, in contrast with the sea
s.c: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between terms which designate land in contrast with water and those which designate cultivated land. Even in English the normal term for land close to water is ‘shore’ or ‘coast,’ and therefore one may translate ⟦Matthew 14:24|Matthew 14:24⟧ as ‘the boat was already far away from the shore.’ Similarly, in ⟦Acts 27:27|Acts 27:27⟧ one may translate ‘we were getting close to shore.’

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Sociopolitical Areas
s.d: region or regions of the earth, normally in relation to some ethnic group or geographical center, but not necessarily constituting a unit of governmental administration{N:001}
s.g: region; territory; land; district (though this might imply too precisely a governmental area)
s.c: The meanings of γῆ, χώρα, κλίμαὅριον, and μέρος are not to be regarded as completely synonymous, but in certain of their NT usages they are largely overlapping in reference.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Areas Which Are Uninhabited or Only Sparsely Populated
s.d: a rural area in contrast with a population center
s.c: A rural area is often identified by a term or phrase meaning ‘extension of fields’ or ‘place of field after field’ or ‘area of farms.’

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Pastures and Cultivated Lands
s.d: land under cultivation or used for pasture

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Political
s.d: the inhabitants of a region{N:002}
s.c: In a number of languages it is quite impossible to speak of ‘a region going out’ (⟦Mark 1:5|Mark 1:5⟧), since the term for ‘region’ cannot substitute for ‘the people of the region.’ Therefore, all such references must be made personal.

s.dp: Linear Movement › Move, Come/Go
s.d: to move on from one place to another
s.c: In translating ⟦Matthew 15:17|Matthew 15:17⟧ it may be necessary to add an element which suggests swallowing, since something which enters a person’s mouth does not automatically go into the stomach. Accordingly, it may be necessary to translate ‘anything that goes into a person’s mouth and is swallowed goes on then into his stomach.’ It would also be possible to say ‘anything that goes into one’s throat goes on then into a person’s stomach.’|In ⟦John 8:37|John 8:37⟧ χωρέω appears to be used figuratively in the statement ὁ λόγος ὁ ἐμὸς οὐ χωρεῖ ἐν ὑμῖν ‘my word makes no progress in you,’ but it is also possible to interpret χωρέω in this context as referring to an adequate place, for example, ‘my word finds no room in you’ (see LN 80.4).

s.dp: Space › Space, Place
s.d: to be a quantity of space
s.g: to have room for; to be space for; to contain

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Accept As True
s.d: to be able to accept a message and respond accordingly
s.g: to be able to accept; to receive
s.c: It is possible to understand χωρέω in ⟦Matthew 19:11|Matthew 19:11⟧ as meaning ‘to be able to understand.’

s.dp: Association › Associate
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:χωρέω<SDBG:χωρέω:000001>}[b] ‘to have room for,’ {D:80.4}) to be friendly disposed toward someone
s.g: to open one’s heart to; to be friendly to

s.dp: Whole, Unite, Part, Divide › Separate
s.d: to separate objects by introducing considerable space or isolation
s.g: to separate; to isolate one from another

s.dp: Association › Marriage, Divorce
s.d: to dissolve the marriage bond
s.c: Expressions for divorce are often based on terms meaning literally ‘to send away,’ ‘to separate from,’ or ‘to leave one another.’ However, in a number of languages idiomatic expressions are employed, for example ‘to send him off with his clothes,’ ‘to untie the knot between them,’ or ‘to throw away her hearthstones.’|Some persons have attempted to make an important distinction between ἀφίημι in ⟦1 Corinthians 7:11|1 Corinthians 7:11⟧ and χωρίζω in ⟦1 Corinthians 7:15|1 Corinthians 7:15⟧ on the assumption that ἀφίημι implies legal divorce, while χωρίζω only relates to separation. Such a distinction, however, seems to be quite artificial.

s.dp: Linear Movement › Leave, Depart, Flee, Escape, Send
s.d: to separate from, as the result of motion away from

s.dp: Existence in Space › Put, Place
s.d: to cause to be at a distance
s.g: to remove at a distance; to separate considerably

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Pastures and Cultivated Lands
s.d: land under cultivation or used for pasture

s.dp: Relations › Dissociation
s.d: a marker of negatively linked elements{N:001}
s.g: without; not with; no relationship to; apart from; independent of
s.c: It would be wrong to restructure ⟦John 1:3|John 1:3⟧ to read ‘he made everything in all creation,’ for in the Scriptures God is spoken of as the Creator, but the creation was done ‘through the Word.’ If one must restructure ⟦John 1:3|John 1:3⟧, it may be possible to say ‘he was involved in everything that was created’ or ‘he took part in creating everything.’|In ⟦1 Corinthians 11:11|1 Corinthians 11:11⟧ χωρίς does not specify the particular relationship but only indicates the lack of relationship or involvement. This, of course, is negated by οὔτε, so that one may translate this portion of ⟦1 Corinthians 11:11|1 Corinthians 11:11⟧ as ‘nor is woman without some relationship to man, nor is man without relationship to woman.’ In view of the overall context, one may then render the passage simply as ‘woman is not independent of man, nor is man independent of woman.’ In some languages, however, it may be necessary of ‘wife’ and ‘husband,’ since terms for ‘man’ or ‘woman’ may be wrongly interpreted in a strictly erotic sense.|Because of the double negation of ⟦1 Corinthians 11:11|1 Corinthians 11:11⟧, in some languages it may be necessary to employ a positive equivalent, for example, ‘for woman is dependent on man and man is dependent on woman’ or ‘a wife is dependent on her husband and a husband is dependent on his wife.’|The expression ‘apart from any works’ in ⟦Romans 4:6|Romans 4:6⟧ may be rendered in some languages as ‘and what a person does, does not count’ or ‘and this is not because of what one does.’

s.dp: Whole, Unite, Part, Divide › Separate
s.d: to something which occurs separately or by itself

s.dp: Spacial Orientations › North, South, East, West
s.d: the direction between north and west
s.c: The difference in expression is due to designating the directions of the wind either as the direction from which the wind comes or the direction toward which the wind blows. See commentaries.|In rendering directions which are not cardinal points, one may often use a variety of expressions, for example, ‘between north and west’ or ‘from the north a little west’ or ‘to the north of west.’ A high percentage of languages designate directions by reference to the rising and setting of the sun. Accordingly, ⟦Acts 27:12|Acts 27:12⟧ may be rendered as ‘a harbor that is open to the sea to the left of the setting sun and to the right of the setting sun.’

s.dp: Communication › Sing, Lament
s.d: to sing songs of praise, with the possible implication of instrumental accompaniment (in the NT often related to the singing of OT psalms)
s.g: to sing; to sing a psalm; to sing a song of praise; to sing praises

s.dp: Communication › Sing, Lament
s.d: a song of praise (in the NT probably a reference to an OT psalm)

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Religious
s.d: an individual who pretends to be a close member of a socio-religious group but is not (see {D:11.22}, {D:11.23}, and {D:11.24})
s.g: false brother; one who only pretends to be a fellow believer in Christ
s.c: It is frequently necessary to make explicit the full implications of ‘false brother’ by translating ‘one who pretends to be a fellow believer in Christ but is not.’

s.dp: Religious Activities › Roles and Functions
s.d: one who claims to be an apostle but is not

s.dp: Communication › Speak Truth, Speak Falsehood
s.d: (derivative of {L:ψεύδομαι<SDBG:ψεύδομαι:000000>} ‘to lie,’ {D:33.253}) one who utters falsehoods and lies
s.c: Since lying is a universal, there is usually no difficulty in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘liar,’ though frequently the equivalent is an idiomatic expression, for example, ‘to speak too much,’ ‘to speak with two tongues,’ or ‘to speak what is not one’s thoughts.’

s.dp: Communication › Teach
s.d: one who teaches falsehoods
s.g: false teacher; teacher of what is a lie
s.c: In rendering ψευδοδιδάσκαλος, it is important to avoid an expression which will simply mean that a person pretends to be a teacher and is not. What is important here is that the individual teaches what is not true.

s.dp: Communication › Speak Truth, Speak Falsehood
s.d: one who utters falsehoods and lies
s.c: Since lying is a universal, there is usually no difficulty in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘liar,’ though frequently the equivalent is an idiomatic expression, for example, ‘to speak too much,’ ‘to speak with two tongues,’ or ‘to speak what is not one’s thoughts.’

s.dp: Communication › Speak Truth, Speak Falsehood
s.d: to communicate what is false, with the evident purpose of misleading
s.c: The Greek term ψεύδομαι and the English equivalent ‘to lie’ involve more than simply telling what is not true, for this could occur without an intent to deceive or mislead. ψεύδομαι, therefore, involves not only the communication of a falsehood but also the intent to deceive.

s.dp: Communication › Witness, Testify
s.d: to provide a false or untrue witness
s.g: to give false witness; to testify falsely
s.c: A person who gives false witness may deceive in two aspects, (1) in pretending to have been an eyewitness to an event and (2) in saying what is not true, but the focal element in ψευδομαρτυρέω is the fact that what is said is not true.

s.dp: Communication › Witness, Testify
s.d: (derivative of {L:ψευδομαρτυρέω<SDBG:ψευδομαρτυρέω:000000>} ‘to testify falsely,’ {D:33.271}) the content of what is testified falsely

s.dp: Communication › Witness, Testify
s.d: (derivative of {L:ψευδομαρτυρέω<SDBG:ψευδομαρτυρέω:000000>} ‘to testify falsely,’ {D:33.271}) one who testifies falsely
s.c: The focal element in the evidence provided by a ‘false witness’ is the fact that what is said is not true.|It is also possible that such a person has pretended to have been present and thus an eyewitness of an event, but that is not the focus of the meaning. In fact, a false witness may have been present but at the same time may later provide false evidence as to what took place. It is possible to render ψευδόμαρτυς in some languages as ‘one who pretends to know about something but is really lying in what he says’ or ‘one who lies about what he pretends to have seen.’

s.dp: Religious Activities › Roles and Functions
s.d: one who claims to be a prophet and is not and thus proclaims what is false

s.dp: Communication › Speak Truth, Speak Falsehood
s.d: (derivative of {L:ψεύδομαι<SDBG:ψεύδομαι:000000>} ‘to lie,’ {D:33.253}) the content of a false utterance

s.dp: Religious Activities › Roles and Functions
s.d: one who claims to be the Christ or the Messiah but is not

s.dp: Communication › Name
s.d: pertaining to being falsely or wrongly called by a name

s.dp: Communication › Speak Truth, Speak Falsehood
s.d: (derivative of {L:ψεύδομαι<SDBG:ψεύδομαι:000000>} ‘to lie,’ {D:33.253}) the content of a false utterance
s.c: It may be important in some instances to restructure the semantic relationships in this clause in ⟦Romans 3:7|Romans 3:7⟧, for example, ‘if my lie makes God’s truth appear more glorious.’

s.dp: Communication › Speak Truth, Speak Falsehood
s.d: one who utters falsehoods and lies
s.c: Since lying is a universal, there is usually no difficulty in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘liar,’ though frequently the equivalent is an idiomatic expression, for example, ‘to speak too much,’ ‘to speak with two tongues,’ or ‘to speak what is not one’s thoughts.’

s.dp: Sensory Events and States › Touch, Feel
s.d: to touch by feeling and handling, implying movement over a surface
s.g: to touch; to feel; to handle; to feel around for
s.c: There are a number of problems involved in the rendering of ⟦1 John 1:1|1 John 1:1⟧, for there are several radical shifts in figurative meaning. The specific reference is to ‘the Word of life’ which seems like a purposely ambiguous reference to Jesus Christ. The statement about ‘hearing the Word’ would seem to refer to a message, but the reference to ‘seeing’ implies some type of object. To emphasize the concrete nature of such an object (namely, the person of Christ), this statement about ‘touching’ is included, but in some languages a reference to ‘feeling and handling’ might imply quite a wrong connotation or even improper activity, particularly if the object involved is specifically a person.

s.dp: Learn › Try To Learn
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ψηλαφάω<SDBG:ψηλαφάω:000000>}[a] ‘to touch, to feel,’ {D:24.76}) to make an effort, despite difficulties, to come to know something, when the chances of success in such an enterprise are not particularly great
s.g: to feel around for; to grope for; to try to find

s.dp: Number › Number, Countless
s.d: to count up or calculate a total
s.g: to count; to calculate; to add up; to figure out
s.c: This process of ‘adding up the number of the beast’ involved calculating the total based upon the numerical values of each of the letters of the name. For another interpretation of ψηφίζω in ⟦Revelation 13:18|Revelation 13:18⟧, see LN 32.15.

s.dp: Understand › Come To Understand
s.d: to come to understand the meaning of something by figuring it out
s.g: to come to understand; to interpret; to figure out
s.c: The third person imperative form ψηφισάτω in ⟦Revelation 13:18|Revelation 13:18⟧ is extremely difficult to render in some languages, and even in English the expression ‘let him understand’ is quite misleading, since it might imply permission rather than polite command. In some languages the equivalent of this third person imperative is an expression such as ‘should understand’ or ‘ought to be able to understand.’ For another interpretation of ψηφίζω in ⟦Revelation 13:18|Revelation 13:18⟧, see LN 60.4.

s.dp: Natural Substances › Earth, Mud, Sand, Rock
s.d: a small stone, possibly used for casting a vote or as a magical amulet
s.c: A number of different suggestions have been made as to the reference of ψῆφος in ⟦Revelation 2:17|Revelation 2:17⟧. Some scholars believe that the white ψῆφος indicates a vote of acquittal in court. Others contend that it is simply a magical amulet; still others, a token of Roman hospitality; and finally, some have suggested that it may represent a ticket to the gladiatorial games, that is to say, to martyrdom. The context, however, suggests clearly that this is something to be prized and a type of reward for those who have ‘won the victory.’

s.dp: Communication › Gossip
s.d: providing harmful information about a person, often spoken in whispers or in low voice, with the implication that such information is not widely known and therefore should presumably be kept secret

s.dp: Communication › Gossip
s.d: one who habitually engages in gossip

s.dp: Foods and Condiments › Food
s.d: a small piece of food (normally bread)
s.c: In ⟦Matthew 15:27|Matthew 15:27⟧, ⟦Mark 7:28|Mark 7:28⟧, and ⟦Luke 16:21|Luke 16:21⟧ (apparatus) the reference is to small crumbs or pieces of food that might fall from the table. In some languages an equivalent is ‘a small bit of food’ or ‘a tiny bite of food.’

s.dp: Psychological Faculties
s.d: the essence of life in terms of thinking, willing, and feeling
s.g: inner self; mind; thoughts; feelings; heart; being
s.c: It is also possible to render ψυχή in ⟦Philippians 1:27|Philippians 1:27⟧ as ‘purpose’ or ‘desire,’ for ψυχή focuses upon the total psychological being involved in struggling for the faith.|ψυχή is often glossed as ‘heart’ or ‘desire.’ Compare the following: περίλυπός ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή μου ἕως θανάτου ‘my heart is sorrowful even to the point of death’ ⟦Matthew 26:38|Matthew 26:38⟧; ἵνα μὴ κάμητε ταῖς ψυχαῖς ὑμῶν ἐκλυόμενοι ‘so do not let your hearts become discouraged and give up’ ⟦Hebrews 12:3|Hebrews 12:3⟧ (for ψυχή in the idiom κάμνω τῇ ψυχῇ, see LN 25.291); ἀλλ ὡς δοῦλοι Χριστοῦ ποιοῦντες τὸ θέλημα τοῦ θεοῦ ἐκ ψυχῆς ‘but with all your heart, do what God wants, as slaves of Christ’ ⟦Ephesians 6:6|Ephesians 6:6⟧. In these passages, however, ψυχή refers really to the entire being of a person, so that ⟦Matthew 26:38|Matthew 26:38⟧ may very well be rendered as ‘my sorrow is so great it almost kills me.’ ⟦Hebrews 12:3|Hebrews 12:3⟧ may also be rendered as ‘so do not let yourselves be discouraged and give up,’ and ⟦Ephesians 6:6|Ephesians 6:6⟧ may be appropriately rendered as ‘but with your whole being, do what God wants, as slaves of Christ.’|The meaning of ψυχή in the sense of the person as an individual is treated under ψυχή (LN 9.20) as, for example, in ⟦Matthew 11:29|Matthew 11:29⟧ (εὑρήσετε ἀνάπαυσιν ταῖς ψυχαῖς ὑμῶν ‘you will find rest for yourselves’).|Even in those contexts in which ψυχή refers to existence beyond death, it may be referring figuratively to the person. For example, in ⟦Acts 2:27|Acts 2:27⟧ (οὐκ ἐγκαταλείψεις τὴν ψυχήν μου εἰς ᾅδην one may translate ‘you will not abandon my soul to Hades’ or ‘you will not abandon me to the grave.’|It is important to distinguish ψυχή, signifying a psychological faculty, from ψυχή, meaning ‘physical life, life principle’ (LN 23.88). Note, for example, the occurrence of ψυχή in ⟦Hebrews 4:12|Hebrews 4:12⟧ (διϊκνούμενος ἄχρι μερισμοῦ ψυχῆς καὶ πνεύματος ‘it cuts all the way through to where physical life and spirit meet’). Note also the occurrence of ψυχή in ⟦1 Thessalonians 5:23|1 Thessalonians 5:23⟧ αὐτὸς δὲ ὁ θεὸς τῆς εἰρήνης ἁγιάσαι ὑμᾶς ὁλοτελεῖς, καὶ ὁλόκληρον ὑμῶν τὸ πνεῦμα καὶ ἡ ψυχὴ καὶ τὸ σῶμα ἀμέμπτως ἐν τῇ παρουσίᾳ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ τηρηθείη ‘may the God who gives us peace make you holy in every way and keep your whole being - spirit, life, and body - free from all fault at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ’).|In certain contexts ψυχή would appear to be in contrast with καρδία (LN 26.3) and διάνοια (LN 26.14) as, for example, in ⟦Matthew 22:37|Matthew 22:37⟧ ἀγαπήσεις κύριον τὸν θεόν σου ἐν ὅλω τῇ καρδίᾳ σου καὶ ἐν ὅλω τῇ ψυχῇ σου καὶ ἐν ὅλω τῇ διανοίᾳ σου ‘you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and soul and mind’). Because of the three terms, some have insisted that there must be at least three quite different parts of human personality. Others, however, have concluded that instead of being three parts of personality, these are only three different perspectives which one may employ in thinking about or describing human personality. Still others would contend that the use of the three terms, καρδία, ψυχή and διάνοια, only emphasizes the totality of human personality, and no clear-cut distinctions can possibly be made. Certainly the referents involve considerable overlapping. One could translate with complete justification ⟦Matthew 22:37|Matthew 22:37⟧ as ‘you shall love the Lord with all your heart and life and mind.’ In fact, in many languages it is impossible to distinguish between καρδία, ψυχή, and διάνοια, and therefore it may be necessary to translate as ‘you shall love the Lord your God with all that you desire and with all that you think’ or ‘you must love the Lord your God with all your being.’

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: the existence of a human being, or other living creature, sustained by the presence of air to breathe and food to eat
s.c: In rendering ψυχή in ⟦Romans 11:3|Romans 11:3⟧ it may be necessary to indicate more precisely the relationship between ‘to seek’ and ‘life,’ for example, ‘they seek to destroy my life’ or ‘they seek to cause me no longer to live.’|In a number of languages there is no noun-like word for ‘life.’ It may therefore be necessary to change all passages which speak of ‘life’ into a corresponding expression using a verb-like form meaning ‘to live.’

s.dp: People › Human Beings
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ψυχή<SDBG:ψυχή:000000>}[a] ‘inner self, mind,’ {D:26.4}) a person as a living being{N:001}

s.dp: Animals
s.d: (an idiom, literally: living soul) any living creature, whether animal or human
s.c: Though the phrase ψυχὴ ζωῆς is highly generic in meaning, its specific reference in ⟦Revelation 16:3|Revelation 16:3⟧ is to creatures of the sea, and therefore in most languages one must translate simply ‘fish’ or ‘that which lives in the sea.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Sorrow, Regret
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to be tormented in soul) to experience mental torment involving sorrow mixed with anger
s.g: to experience anguish; to be tormented in one’s heart

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Hate, Hateful
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to cause a person’s attitude to be bad against) to cause someone to have hostile feelings of dislike toward someone
s.g: to turn someone against; to cause to dislike

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Discouragement
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to become tired in spirit) to gradually lose one’s motivation to accomplish some goal
s.g: to become discouraged; to become tired of

s.dp: Danger, Risk, Safe, Save › Cause To Be Safe, Free from Danger
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to acquire one’s soul or to acquire one’s life) to save oneself from grave danger or death
s.g: to save oneself; to protect oneself

s.dp: Danger, Risk, Safe, Save › Expose Oneself to Danger
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to hand over life) to expose oneself willingly to a danger or risk
s.g: to risk; to risk one’s life
s.c: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘risking one’s life’ is ‘exposing oneself to death’ or ‘showing that one is willing to die’ or ‘walking into the danger of dying.’

s.dp: Danger, Risk, Safe, Save › Cause To Be Safe, Free from Danger
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to do something with regard to one’s life) to save or preserve one’s own life
s.g: to save one’s life; to save oneself

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Sorrow, Regret
s.d: (an idiom, literally: a sword goes through one’s soul) to feel the intense pain of sorrow
s.g: to feel pain and sorrow; to be sorrowful and distressed

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to lay down one’s life) to die, with the implication of voluntary or willing action
s.g: to die voluntarily; to die willingly
s.c: Though in English the phrases ‘to lay down one’s life’ or ‘to give one’s life’ do suggest a voluntary dying, a literal rendering of such expressions in other languages would not necessarily imply the same. It may therefore be necessary to use such expressions as ‘to die willingly’ or ‘to die without resisting.’ In some languages ‘willingly’ is expressed primarily as a negation of objecting, for example, ‘I will not object to dying.’

s.dp: Features of Objects › Physical [Material], Spiritual
s.d: pertaining to being material or physical, especially in relation to life processes
s.c: In some languages, however, it is impossible to translate σπείρεται in ⟦1 Corinthians 15:44|1 Corinthians 15:44⟧ as ‘sown,’ and one must therefore translate this expression as ‘when buried, it is a physical body.’

s.dp: Features of Objects › Natural [Human], Spiritual
s.d: pertaining to human nature (possibly contrasting with {L:σάρκινος<SDBG:σάρκινος:000002>}[c] and {L:σαρκικός<SDBG:σαρκικός:000002>}[c] ‘natural, human,’ {D:79.4}, in focusing somewhat more on so-called higher endowments of personality)
s.c: For another interpretation of ψυχικός in ⟦1 Corinthians 2:14|1 Corinthians 2:14⟧, see LN 41.41.

s.dp: Behavior and Related States › Particular Patterns of Behavior
s.d: (derivative of {L:ψυχή<SDBG:ψυχή:000000>}[a] ‘inner self,’ {D:26.4}) pertaining to behavior which is typical of human nature, in contrast with that which is under the control of God’s Spirit
s.c: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘unspiritual’ is simply ‘one who is not guided by God’s Spirit’ or ‘one who does not live in accordance with God’s Spirit.’ For another interpretation of ψυχικός in ⟦1 Corinthians 2:14|1 Corinthians 2:14⟧, see LN 79.5.

s.dp: Features of Objects › Hot, Lukewarm, Cold
s.d: pertaining to being cold, as of weather conditions

s.dp: Features of Objects › Hot, Lukewarm, Cold
s.d: pertaining to being cold, as of objects and masses

s.dp: Degree › More Than, Less Than [Comparative Degree]
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of ψύχομαι ‘to become cold,’ not occurring in the NT) to diminish significantly in intensity
s.g: to diminish greatly; to become cold

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Eat, Drink
s.d: to cause someone to eat
s.g: to feed; to give to eat

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Give
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ψωμίζω<SDBG:ψωμίζω:000000>}[a] ‘to feed, to give to eat,’ {D:23.5}) to give away or dole out, with the probable implication of bit by bit
s.g: to give away; to dole out

s.dp: Foods and Condiments › Food
s.d: a small piece or bit of bread
s.g: a piece of bread; a bit of bread
s.c: In ⟦John 13:26|John 13:26⟧ it may be necessary to use a phrase such as ‘a broken-off piece of bread’; otherwise the inference might be that the ψωμίον was simply a scrap or crumb of bread. In some languages the appropriate equivalent of ψωμίον in this type of context is ‘a bite of bread.’

s.dp: Physical Impact › Press
s.d: to rub something under pressure to make it smaller
s.c: By rubbing the heads of wheat, the disciples were able to remove the chaff and the so-called ‘beards,’ the stiff projections arising from each kernel. This process would be equivalent to threshing and would thus be condemned by the Pharisees as work on the Sabbath.

s.dp: Discourse Markers › Marker of Direct Address
s.d: a marker of direct address (functionally equivalent to the traditional vocative)
s.c: Often left untranslated.
